captions: This morning, our pre-market brief leaned positive —
a firm-to-positive open, on a strong US lead.
But the market did the opposite.
It crashed for a third straight day.
So let's be honest,
and analyse exactly what went wrong and why.
Here's the twist —
the one thing our pre-market brief flagged as the key risk is exactly what brought the market down.
This is information analysis, not investment advice.
First, the damage.
The Sensex crashed seven hundred fifteen points to close at seventy-six thousand seven hundred fifty-five —
down almost a percent.
The Nifty fell one hundred ninety-one points to twenty-three thousand nine hundred ninety-six —
closing below the key twenty-four thousand mark.
And the Bank Nifty was the worst hit,
down one point two three percent.
This was the third straight down day,
and the steepest fall in nearly two weeks.
Unlike yesterday, there was no midcap cushion —
the selling was broad-based across the market.
So why did it crash?
Four reasons — and the first one is the whole story.
Number one — crude oil.
Brent crude jumped four point six eight percent to ninety-five point two seven dollars,
a five-week high, as the West Asia conflict escalated.
India imports most of its oil,
so this is the trigger that hit everything.
Number two — a bank selloff.
The Bank Nifty fell one point two three percent, with S-B-I,
I-C-I-C-I and Axis dragging financials down for a third straight day.
Number three — the selling was broad-based.
I-T, pharma and realty all bled.
Unlike yesterday, no sector was spared.
Number four — the backdrop.
Fresh Middle East escalation and US tariff fears kept global markets in a risk-off mood.
Now the biggest losers.
The top loser was InterGlobe Aviation — IndiGo.
This makes perfect sense: airlines are hit hardest by a crude spike,
because jet fuel is their single biggest cost.
Next, the banks — S-B-I, I-C-I-C-I and Axis.
The banking selloff was the single biggest drag on the index.
Then Infosys and Jio Financial.
Note this carefully —
I-T fell even though the Nasdaq was strong overnight.
Crude and geopolitics completely overrode the tech tailwind we expected.
And Doctor Reddy's stayed weak for a second day,
with UltraTech Cement also among the laggards.
It wasn't all red.
A few names held up — and the pattern is a lesson in itself.
Bajaj Auto and TVS Motor actually rose, defying the selloff,
on their strong quarterly results —
exactly the earnings reaction we flagged this morning.
Defensive consumer names like Hindustan Unilever and Titan held up,
as money rotated to safety.
And utilities — N-T-P-C and Power Grid — stayed steady,
because they're rate-insensitive and shielded from crude.
The pattern is clear: in a crude-driven crash,
money hides in defensives, utilities,
and genuine earnings beats.
Now the honest review — what we expected this morning,
versus what actually happened.
We expected a firm, positive open on a strong US lead.
Instead, crude spiked and the market crashed for a third day.
We thought the Nasdaq's one point three percent jump would lift Indian I-T.
Instead, Infosys and I-T fell —
crude and geopolitics overrode that tailwind completely.
But here's the key point —
this morning we explicitly flagged crude near ninety dollars as the number-one risk.
And that exact risk is what dominated the entire day.
That's the real lesson: a pre-market brief is a setup,
not a forecast.
Overnight cues can be wiped out by a single geopolitical shock —
and the risk you flag can be the one that decides the day.
So, five lessons from today.
One — a pre-market brief is a setup, not a forecast.
The risk you flag can be the very thing that wins the day.
Two — geopolitical shocks, like a crude spike,
can override overnight cues within minutes of the open.
Three — crude near ninety-five dollars hurts airlines,
paint companies and oil marketers the most.
Watch those.
Four — in a broad selloff, defensives,
utilities and genuine earnings-beats are where money hides.
Five — for a long-term S-I-P investor,
a three-day dip is still just noise.
Don't panic-sell into a geopolitical scare.
July twenty-second, at a glance.
The Sensex fell seven hundred fifteen points and the Nifty broke below twenty-four thousand —
the third straight down day.
The cause —
crude jumping almost five percent to ninety-five dollars,
a bank selloff, and Middle East escalation.
The losers — IndiGo, S-B-I, I-C-I-C-I, Infosys,
and Doctor Reddy's.
The winners — Bajaj Auto, T-V-S,
and defensives like Hindustan Unilever and N-T-P-C.
And the lesson — the risk we flagged this morning, crude,
is exactly what hit.
A pre-market is a setup, not a promise — and today,
the flagged risk won.
This information is aggregated from public sources —
for analysis only, not investment advice.
Thanks for watching, and see you at tomorrow's open.
